   K-Pop giants position for China return after decade-long freeze

 Published   Nov 19, 2026, 12:30 PM

 Set as preferred source Listen Summarise South Korean entertainment firms are preparing for China’s return after Lee Jae Myung and Xi Jinping agreed to expand cultural exchanges and wider trade ties.
 Shares in CJ ENM, JYP, SM and Hybe rose, but the deal did not clearly reopen K-pop concerts, banned since 2016 after the US missile defence dispute.
 Companies have built China partnerships and units, as a reopening could boost earnings by about 40% and give South Korea’s strained content industry a major new market.
 AI generated
 SEOUL – South Korean entertainment companies are positioning themselves for a return to China after the two countries agreed to expand cultural exchanges, raising hopes that Beijing may loosen restrictions that have kept major K-pop acts out of the mainland for almost a decade.
 Entertainment stocks jumped on the morning of Nov 19 after South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Chinese President Xi Jinping met the day before and said they would work to boost cultural ties.
 The countries will expand a free-trade agreement, including better treatment for South Korean films and games and expanded co-productions of dramas, animation and variety shows. 
 CJ ENM shares jumped more than 20%, JYP Entertainment was up 2%, and SM Entertainment gained around 7%. Hybe – the agency of K-pop megastars BTS – also rose as much as 7% after the market opened on Nov 19.
 The deal, however, stopped short of explicitly opening the door to K-pop concerts, which have been kept out of the mainland since 2016, when China imposed an informal ban on Korean entertainment after Seoul allowed the deployment of a US missile defence system on its territory.
 Xi said his country was willing to carry out “healthy and beneficial” cultural exchanges with South Korea gradually, an emphasis that raises questions about Beijing’s attitude towards K-pop.
 The leadership has previously been wary of the toxic “fandom culture” around idol groups – and their perceived “effeminacy” that officials have publicly denounced. 
 But any shift could create a substantial prize.
 “If the restrictions are lifted, it would effectively open up a new mega-market,” said Lim Do-young, an analyst at Daol Investment & Securities.
 China’s concert market is about 85% the size of Japan’s and 2.8 times that of South Korea’s, he added.
 Because Beijing never formally acknowledged imposing restrictions on Korean entertainment, there may not be an official declaration that they have ended, Lim said.
 Instead, the clearest signal would be the return of large-scale K-pop performances: a concert drawing more than 10,000 people and featuring a full set of at least 15 songs would effectively serve as a test of whether the restrictions have been lifted.
 Korean entertainment companies have spent the past two years preparing for that possibility.
 Hybe has established a Beijing unit, while SM has deepened ties with Tencent Music Entertainment Group, which became its second-largest shareholder.
 CJ ENM , which operates K-pop concerts and drama studios, has also teamed up with JYP’s Chinese unit and Tencent Music in a venture to develop artists for Greater China.
 The partnerships point to a changing model for Korean companies seeking access to China, with local partners playing a bigger role in developing artists and managing businesses.
 China is a different entertainment market from what it was a decade ago, when Korean celebrities and television programmes commanded significant attention.
 Its domestic music, known as Mandopop, programming ranging from microdramas to long-form series, and games have expanded rapidly and increasingly found audiences overseas.
 A reopening could also provide a lifeline for South Korea’s content industry, which is grappling with rising production costs and tighter financing.
 South Korean dramas largely disappeared from China’s official streaming platforms and television networks after the restrictions took hold, shutting producers out of what had been a lucrative market.
 Demand never entirely disappeared, however, with some Chinese fans continuing to seek out Korean shows through virtual private networks and unauthorised streaming and download sites.
 If China eventually allows K-pop concerts and Korean variety-show productions while South Korea further eases visa requirements for Chinese visitors, Korean entertainment companies could see earnings rise by about 40%, according to a note by Hana Securities.
 Media companies and businesses exposed to inbound Chinese tourism would also benefit, it said.
 The agreement also comes as Beijing seeks to stimulate domestic consumption with a focus on services, making concerts, tourism and entertainment potential sources of additional spending.
 Compared with developed economies such as the US, services account for a much smaller share of Chinese households’ spending. Officials have repeatedly said that a lack of a quality supply of services is a key issue and pledged to further open up the sector to foreign firms. BLOOMBERG
